La dissymétrie entre ses visiteurs et lui est complète et, à vrai dire, assez incroyable : d'un côté, on vient — avec un respect réel ou feint — voir à quoi ressemble le grand philosophe du moment, déjà légendaire ; de l'autre, on peut deviner les sentiments mêlés de tristesse, de crainte et de soulagement du philosophe rattrapé par son passé, cerné par la malveillance, se découvrant cependant des admirateurs et peut-être des amis inespérés parmi les représentants de la puissance occupante. Un de ses voisins croit-il qu'on vient l'arrêter*? C'est du contraire qu'il s'agit : des actes de reconnaissance et des hommages qui annoncent, pour Heidegger, les compensations constantes qu'il trouvera du côté de la France.

Heidegger lui-même semble si favorablement impressionné par ces visites[^1] qu’il écrit à Jean Beaufret le 23 novembre 1945 : «Je pressens, pour autant que j’aie pu m’en rendre compte en quelques semaines seulement, dans la pensée des jeunes philosophes de France, un élan extraordinaire qui montre bien qu’en ce domaine une révolution se prépare[^2].»

Qu'en est-il effectivement au niveau proprement philosophique ? Au-delà des rumeurs de la mode existentialiste, et à l'exception de Sartre, une écoute philosophique de qualité est-elle discernable dans la France de l'époque ? S'il ne fait pas de doute que la réponse est positive, il faut maintenant en préciser les attendus.
SIGNES D'INTELLIGENCE D'UN CERTAIN M. BEAUFRET

Lors de sa toute première visite au domicile du Maître, Frédéric de Towarnicki remet à Mme Heidegger deux numéros de la revue Confluences où ont tout récemment paru une série d'articles de Jean Beaufret, « À propos de l'existentialisme ». Petite cause, grands effets : cet événement minuscule devait être l'occasion d'une des plus profondes et célèbres amitiés philosophiques de l'histoire !

Sur le moment, Towarnicki lui-même est évidemment loin de se douter des conséquences de ce geste, mais il apprécie les qualités du texte de Beaufret et pressent que Heidegger peut être sensible à l'effort fait pour aborder sa pensée dans ses spécificités sans être fondue au sein de l'horizon sartrien.

C'est faire preuve de flair, en fonction de la seule tenue d'un texte. Il faut le souligner : en cette matière, les relations personnelles ont suivi les lectures philosophiques, non l'inverse. On a parfois suggéré (et sans doute cru de bonne foi) que Heidegger avait écrit sa fameuse Lettre sur l'humanisme, adressée à Jean Beaufret, pour se créer un appui en France, lançant comme une bouée de sauvetage, alors qu'il était si terriblement isolé en Allemagne. Ce dernier point n'est peut-être pas complètement erroné; mais, avant tout, l'attention de Heidegger a été mise en éveil par la lecture d'un texte : cet acte de reconnaissance de la part du lecteur exceptionnel qu'est Heidegger a une valeur unique qui transcende les considérations psychologiques et anecdotiques. Compte tenu de l'empressement d'intellectuels français à venir à Fribourg, Heidegger n'est pas vraiment à court d'« appuis » extérieurs (Sartre n'était-il pas potentiellement le plus impressionnant?"). Ce qui lui manque, beaucoup plus radicalement en cette année 1945, c'est une écoute authentiquement philosophique de son propre chemin de pensée depuis la publication d'Être et temps, qui remonte déjà à plus de quinze ans. Connaissant maintenant les volumes si décisifs des Œuvres complètes qui ponctuent son itinéraire à partir de 1936 — les cours sur Nietzsche et les Beiträge en particulier —, on mesure mieux son extraordinaire isolement spirituel, encore renforcé par les circonstances. N'ayant pratiquement rien publié depuis une quinzaine d'années, bien que poursuivant intensément son « tournant », il n'a aucun véritable interlocuteur ; seuls peut-être quelques anciens étudiants ou collègues, tels Walter Biemel et Eugen Fink, peuvent alors pressentir les enjeux de cette profonde solitude intellectuelle à laquelle Alphonse de Waelhens fait allusion en ces termes assez insolites, dès 1942 : « Il n'est pas certain que le philosophe de Sein und Zeit puisse surmonter un jour la crise de découragement et de lassitude qu'il connaît depuis plusieurs années, au jugement de celui qui pourrait être, s'il le voulait, le plus pénétrant interprète de sa pensée, Eugen Fink ». Quelle intelligence inédite Heidegger discerne-t-il à l'automne de 1945 dans les pages de Jean Beaufret qui lui sont offertes?

Il est difficile, mais non impossible, de se replacer du point de vue de Heidegger en adoptant un instant son attente et sa curiosité. Son regard d'une rapidité extrême a dît d'emblée saisir les qualités évidentes du texte : clarté, absence de jargon et de bavardage, art d'aller à l'essentiel. On sait d'ailleurs, par la mention qu'il en fait dans sa première missive à Jean Beaufret [4], qu'il a particulièrement apprécié (ce qui n'est pas surprenant) la phrase : « Mais si l'allemand a ses ressources, le français a ses limites [5]. »

chapters.title: Prologue Diversity, coherence, and scheme transfers
chapters.path: chapters/001-Prologue Diversity, coherence, and scheme transfers.md
sample_paragraphs: ## Prologue Diversity, coherence, and scheme transfers
2 Prologue to Part One Diversity, coherence, and scheme transfer

Medicine is the most complex field I shall be studying. Qing legislative and judicial practices were far from simple, but criminal trials followed common procedures and referred to a single body of laws that discussed madness and mad acts with consistent terminology. Although Qing laws were often modified, officials worked with only one code. Medical texts form a less cohesive corpus. They were produced in often-obscure contexts by authors or compilers who shared neither a common vocabulary nor a common understanding of madness. With no institution to stabilize it, the meaning of medical terms varied in time, between works of the same period, and even within individual works.[^1] Unlike the relatively simple madness that the law described, medical kuang 狂 was characterized by a wide variety of behaviors and traced to origins as diverse as mucus accumulation in the chest, internally generated Liver Fire, and invasion by external Wind. Many contradictory explanations could even be presented as true in a single text.[^2]

To assess and explain this diversity properly, I pay attention not only to trendsetters and famous doctors, but also to writings that epitomized their age more than they marked it:[^3] primers, florilegia of medical oddities, unpublished collections of medical cases, etc. In addition to painting a more complete image of medical views of madness, this broad approach also deemphasizes the contrast between “elite medicine” and “popular practice” by showing that a large range of literate practitioners lived between these two abstract extremes.
approach also deemphasizes the contrast between “elite medicine” and “popular practice” by showing that a large range of literate practitioners lived between these two abstract extremes.

My broad reading of medical texts will also help to show that although madness was rarely at the core of doctrinal controversies, medical discussions of insanity quickly absorbed new doctrinal developments. The seven chapters of Part One will thus narrate how conceptions of kuang and its related illnesses evolved along with the rest of medical precepts and practices.

Throughout, I use “illness” as a translation of the term bing 病 and as a label for the kinds of disorders that Chinese medicine discussed: clusters of clinically relevant symptoms that were grouped under one particular name. The problem in translating bing is not to determine whether that term really meant “illness,” “disease,” or “disorder,” but to find a rendering that neither clashes with the meaning of bing nor brings undue connotations into our analysis. To some extent, a translation is good because of what it avoids. Translating bing as “illness” will not presuppose that all bing defined in Chinese medical texts were “diseases,” a term that now seems to imply rootedness in biological processes. I also avoid “disorder” because it would make Chinese concepts of madness sound too close to those of the DSM (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders), the influential manual that calls most psychiatric derangements “disorders” (Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder and the like). [4]

There were effectively no “types of madness” in Chinese medicine, just one madness—kuang or diankuang—with many symptoms. Historians usually interpret dian as a form of madness distinct from kuang (see 1: 5n9), but I will argue that a clear symptomatic distinction between dian and kuang only crystallized in the nineteenth century. [5] Kuang referred to various disorders of perception, affect, language, and especially behavior. People were labeled kuang when they lost some or all social competence—a woman ran outside naked, a man became delirious or took himself for a god. Physicians may have focused on patent mad behavior because they were only called to treat men and women whom their relatives saw as patently mad. Most feelings of mental discomfort were probably not reported to doctors, and thus rarely appeared in medical documents. I will call the symptoms of kuang “psycho-behavioral.”

Although madness was defined socially, physicians usually interpreted insane behavior through categories that drew diagnosis away from the patient's daily context. Armed with notions such as "stasis," "depletion," or "Liver Fire," they reduced to organic imbalances problems that had probably developed from social and interpersonal events. Perhaps because of doctors' emphasis on the organic roots of mad behavior, their chief therapeutic goal was usually to stop disabling symptoms rather than to foster a patient's wellbeing. Even physicians who knew that madness had social roots rarely attempted to reinstate their patients into meaningful social relations. They may have judged this to be the family's task. Yet case records remind us that illness meanings were more than organic. As an couched these interpretations also owed much to the strong intertextuality of the Chinese medical tradition. Before they compiled a treatise or a formulary, medical writers had indeed read a large number of treatises and formularies. I will show in Chapter 5 that from the fourteenth century onwards, even the most educated physicians composed treatises by collating excerpts from other medical books. The composition of medical treatises by textual collage favored textual densification around certain issues and thus allowed certain scripts and approaches to be propagated more than others.
task. Yet case records remind us that illness meanings were more than organic. As an affliction that was defined socially, insanity was always more than a bodily event. [6]

Categories and scripts channeled phenomena into intelligible and manageable forms; they also guided perception and suggested methods to tackle the reality they purported to describe. Broadly speaking, medical specialists attributed mad symptoms either to invasion by external forces (“deviant Qi”, Wind, ghosts) or to internal imbalances strong enough to provoke illness.[^4] Doctors claimed they could cure their patients by expelling these external invaders or redressing these pathogenic imbalances. Because of this emphasis on dynamic situations and a general therapeutic optimism, the medical tradition considered permanent disorders anomalous. Chinese physicians therefore rarely medicalized personality and almost never called patients “madmen” (狂人 or 瘋子).

The medical scripts by which doctors understood madness changed significantly between the eighth and the fourteenth century, and again from the fourteenth to the sixteenth century. I plan to demonstrate that new explanations and treatments for insanity often borrowed from the prototypical scenarios of other illnesses or from contemporaneous interpretations of human vitality rather than from the observation of mad patients. A formal analysis would show that this kind of “scheme transfer” (Bourdieu 1990: 250) was the main mode of change in medical understandings of madness throughout imperial history.

But it was of course people—physicians—who tried to explain madness by borrowing scripts from other illnesses or who drew on current conceptions of vitality to treat insane symptoms in new ways. They based their interpretations on clinical experience, observed symptoms, and deductions from familiar concepts, but the way in which they couched these interpretations also owed much to the strong intertextuality of the Chinese medical tradition. Before they compiled a treatise or a formulary, medical writers had indeed read a large number of treatises and formularies. I will show in Chapter 5 that from the fourteenth century onwards, even the most educated physicians composed treatises by collating excerpts from other medical books. The composition of medical treatises by textual collage favored textual densification around certain issues and thus allowed certain scripts and approaches to be propagated more than others.

Before they compiled a treatise or a formulary, medical writers had indeed read a large number of treatises and formularies. I will show in Chapter 5 that from the fourteenth century onwards, even the most educated physicians composed treatises by collating excerpts from other medical books. The composition of medical treatises by textual collage favored textual densification around certain issues and thus allowed certain scripts and approaches to be propagated more than others.

One major repository of medical arguments throughout imperial history was the Yellow Emperor's Inner Canon (Huangdi neijing 黄帝内經), the earliest versions of which were compiled in the first century BCE on the basis of earlier materials.[^5] Although the text of its main versions was stabilized in the eleventh century,[^6] the parts of the Canon that doctors considered central to medical thinking changed drastically. Liu Wansu 劉完素 (ca. 1120-1200), for example, relied on a short passage from pian 74 of the Basic Questions to argue that most illnesses were caused by Fire and Heat (4.1). Zhang Congzheng 張從正 (1156-1228), for his part, built his notion of “therapy by counter-affect” on the dynamics of Qi as described in pian 5 of the Basic Questions (4.2) whereas Li Gao 李昪 (1181-1251) found other excerpts to support his view that a man's vitality depended on the health of his stomach (4.3). When they eulogized “the Inner Canon,” writers were not referring to an invariant book, but to the precepts that their own interpretive tradition identified as central. The authority of the Canon was thus rarely questioned, but no doctor ever followed all of its precepts.

Where physicians displayed remarkable stability was in the way they described madness. Borrowing formulations from the Inner Canon, medical writers described the symptoms of kuang with roughly the same words from the first century BCE to the late nineteenth century, probably assuming that readers would immediately recognize these words and what they referred to. Chapter 3, to which we now turn, begins by explaining how the two main versions of the Inner Canon described the symptoms of madness.

chapters.title: Psycho-behavioral pathology in Chinese medicine Concepts and early developments, 2nd century BCE – ca. 1150
chapters.path: chapters/002-Psycho-behavioral pathology in Chinese medicine Concepts and early developments, 2nd century BCE – ca 1150.md
sample_paragraphs: ## Psycho-behavioral pathology in Chinese medicine Concepts and early developments, 2nd century BCE – ca. 1150
Psycho-behavioral pathology in Chinese medicine
Concepts and early developments, $ 3^{rd} $ century BCE – ca. 1150

This chapter provides conceptual and factual tools for understanding how medical treatments of insanity changed despite how stably Chinese doctors kept describing mad behavior. As I pointed out in Chapter 1, Chinese people called “mad” the same disorders of behavior, speech, affect, and perception that we intuitively include under the category of madness. Here I survey the way ancient medical texts described such symptoms and analyze how physicians explained and treated psycho-behavioral pathology before about 1150.

I start by examining the prototypical symptoms of kuang as defined in the Yellow Emperor's Inner Canon (first century BCE), a pivotal corpus from which medical writers drew their descriptions of madness for most of imperial history. I then criticize the way modern scholars have used "mental illness" as a foil against which to define Chinese approaches, or even as a reason to refuse comparisons between psychiatry and Chinese medicine. As I shall argue, Chinese medicine and modern psychiatry are comparable because both purport to explain and treat psycho-behavioral symptoms. As I explain next, Chinese doctors assumed that mental activities "supervened" upon organic processes. [1] This is the most critical feature of Chinese medical approaches to insanity. I then map the relations between kuang and proximate illnesses in a seventh-century treatise that attributed most psycho-behavioral pathologies to harmful Winds. The fourth section explains how dian (瑱, 顛, or 癲)—"seizure sickness"—came to refer to insanity by borrowing from non-medical usage.

The second half of this chapter traces how the growing prominence of mucus as a cause of illness starting in the eleventh century deeply altered the way in which Chinese physicians understood and handled madness. I first describe the origins of the notion of “mucus,” a pathological fluid that was not mentioned in the Inner Canon. I then review how the medical activism and publishing activities of the northern-Song government (976-1127) helped to create a pool of common references that facilitated medical debates and intertextual borrowings. For example, many Song doctors debated the claim made in a government-sponsored formulary that “Wind strokes” could be treated with vomit-inducing (“emetic”) drugs. Just around the same time (the turn of the twelfth century), these mucus-targeting emetics were starting to be used to treat madness. 3.1 The kuang 狂 core in the Yellow Emperor corpus

Modern scholars agree that the Yellow Emperor's Inner Canon (Huangdi neijing 黄帝内經) was "an unintegrated compilation of short writings" (Sivin 1995f: 191). Its received versions—the Grand Basis, the Basic Questions, and the Divine Pivot, all of which date to the seventh century or later but were compiled from sources as early as the third century BCE[2]—were "simply different collections of similar material. Any one collection therefore represented the end of one lineage of collecting, as if frozen in time" (Lo 2002: xxix).

The Inner Canon was the most important textual corpus in the history of Chinese medicine. For most of the two millennia that followed its first compilation (in the first century BCE), it served to doctors and medical writers as a repository of authoritative explanations and doctrinal statements. [3] Elite physicians from the eleventh to the twentieth century proclaimed it should form the core of medical education. The diversity of views contained in the Canon allowed a number of rival doctrines hinging on it to claim authenticity.

explanations and doctrinal statements. [3] Elite physicians from the eleventh to the twentieth century proclaimed it should form the core of medical education. The diversity of views contained in the Canon allowed a number of rival doctrines hinging on it to claim authenticity.
One influential passage on madness in the Inner Canon has been traced to the earlier
Cauterization Canon of the Eleven Yin and Yang Vessels (Yinyang shiyi mai jiu jing 陰陽十一脈灸

經), a work of the late third century BCE that described the disorders that occurred when eleven distinct vessels (脈) “stirred” or “were stirred” (動).[4] A few lines on the “YangBrilliance” (陽明) vessel later found their way into a section of the Basic Questions that later physicians liked to cite when they described kuang.[5]

When this [vessel] is moved, one ails from: shivers and ailing from coldness; fondness for stretching; continual yawning, blackness in the center of the forehead; ailing from swelling; when severe, detestation for people and fire; when hearing the sound of wood, panicked alarm; panicky heart; the desire to close doors and windows and dwell in isolation; when the ailment is severe, the desire to mount high and sing, and to cast off clothing and run. These constitute shin reversal. For these [ailments], the Yang-Brilliance vessel controls the treatment.
是勤〔動〕則病 洒洒 病塞＜寒＞ 喜信〔伸〕 數吹〔欠〕 嬿〔顏〕 墨 病種〔腫〕 至則惡人與火 聞木音則狄〔惕〕 然驚 心惕然欲獨必戶牖而處 病甚則欲乘高而歌 棄衣而走 此為骭蹶〔厥〕 是陽明脈主治
Note the seamless transition between what we could call physical and behavioral symptoms. [6]
Two passages from the Basic Questions appear to have been comments on the above.

Pian 49 (“Elucidations on Vessels” 脈解篇) explained: “when the ailment is severe, one desires to mount high and sing, and to cast off clothing and run’ [means that] Yin and Yang [Qi] resume their fight, and they pile on Yang on the outside, [7] making one shed clothes and run” (所謂病至則欲乘高而歌棄衣而走者 陰陽復爭而外並於陽 故使之棄衣而走也; 13.11b). Another gloss in the form of a conversation between the Yellow Emperor and an advisor appeared in pian 30 (“Elucidations on the Yang-Brilliance Vessel” 陽明脈解篇): [8]

“When the illness is serious, [one] discards clothes and runs about, mounts heights and sings. One may even not eat for several days. One will leap walls and ascend rooftops. One would not be able to climb [in such a way] ordinarily, yet when one is ill one unexpectedly can. Why is this?” Qibo said: “The four limbs are the root of all Yang [vessels]. When Yang is flourishing, the four limbs are replete, which makes one able to climb high.” The Yellow Emperor said: “Why does one shed clothes and run?” Qibo said: “When Heat is flourishing in the body, one sheds clothes and wants to run.” The Yellow Emperor: “Why does [the afflicted person] speak wildly, scold close or distant relatives indiscriminately, and sing?” Qibo: “Abundance of Yang makes one speak wildly, scold and revile without discriminating between close and distant relatives, and feel no desire to eat. Having no desire to eat, one runs wildly.”
病甚则棄衣而走 登高而歌 或至不食數日 踰垣上屋 所上之處 皆非其素所能也 病反能者何也 岐伯曰 四支者 諸陽之本也 陽盛則四支實實則能登高也 帝曰 其棄衣而走者何也 岐伯曰 熱盛於身 故棄衣欲走也 帝曰 其妄言罵詈不避親踈而歌者何也 岐伯曰 陽盛則使人妄言罵詈不避親踈而不欲食 不欲食 故妄走也
This passage cast aside physical ills and replaced them with behavioral symptoms: refusal to eat, indiscriminate scolding, and climbing walls and ascending roofs.

chapters.title: From Wind to mucus and Fire The innovations of Jin and Yuan physicians, ca. 1150-1360
chapters.path: chapters/003-From Wind to mucus and Fire The innovations of Jin and Yuan physicians, ca 1150-1360.md
sample_paragraphs: ## From Wind to mucus and Fire The innovations of Jin and Yuan physicians, ca. 1150-1360
From Wind to mucus and Fire The innovations of Jin and Yuan physicians, ca. 1150-1360

In Chapter 3, I traced the increasingly widespread association of mucus with Wind disorders from the tenth to the twelfth century and showed that several illnesses whose pathomechanisms had been considered close to those of kuang—Wind strokes and xian 痈 seizures—were often treated with anti-mucus remedies by the end of that period. Let me now explain how the mucus-and-Fire etiology of madness that dominated late-imperial conceptions of insanity developed. The mucus-and-Fire script emerged among doctrinally minded physicians who lived in north China under the Jin dynasty (1115-1234), and was consolidated by southern doctors who were influenced by these northerners in the early fourteenth century under the Yuan dynasty (1260-1368), after the Mongol conquest of both the Jin and the southern Song (1127-1279) had re-established contacts between north and south China. The innovations these medical thinkers proposed built on the trends I outlined in Chapter 3, but it was their doctrinal and therapeutic precepts that came to dominate later medical thinking. During these men's lives (and partly thanks to their efforts), "Cold Injury" (shangban 傷寒) replaced "Wind illnesses" as the new dominant class of illnesses.

The way Jin-Yuan physicians interpreted madness and handled mad people depended on their broader understanding of illness and vitality. The development of ColdInjury medicine, for example, enhanced the importance of Heat and Fire as etiological factors and motivated a number of doctors to use Cold-Injury remedies to treat psychobehavioral symptoms.

Part 4.1 discusses Liu Wansu's 劉完素 (ca. 1120-1200) general emphasis on the etiology of Fire and his reinterpretation of "Wind" as a form of Heat. Both reorientations were widely accepted by later physicians. The second section explains why Zhang Congzheng 張從正 (1156-1228) generally treated madness with emetic and purgative remedies drawn from the Treatise on Cold Injury (ca. 200 CE). Zhang's medicine brought together for the first time all the major trends I have described so far: therapeutic focus on mucus, adoption of Cold-injury remedies, and the use of aggressive remedies against madness. The next part discusses how Li Gao's 李杲 (1181-1251) and Wang Haogu's 王好古 (1200?-1264?) identified depletion as a major cause of illness and how Wang applied these views to the treatment of a mad man. Their emphasis on depletion became important to medical understandings of madness from the sixteenth century onwards. As section 4.4 will show, Zhu Zhenheng 朱震亨 (1282-1358) gave a central role to Fire and mucus in the creation of illness and in the production of mad behavior. His doctrinal amalgams defined fifteenth- and sixteenth-century medicine. Part five shows how widespread anti-mucus therapies of madness had become by the mid-fourteenth century. The sixth section explains the bodily mechanisms by which doctors thought mucus could trigger madness. In the conclusion, I explain the collapse of the category of "Wind illnesses" and present a few ideas on what is usually (but misleadingly) called "Jin-Yuan medicine." 4.1 Liu Wansu: the Heat etiology and the decline of Wind
Liu Wansu 劉完素 (ca. 1120–1200) was the first systematizer of the medicine of

Heat and Fire that was eventually applied to madness and many other illnesses that were once attributed to Wind. His ideas on the origins of illness and his therapeutic recommendations occupied a central place in Zhu Zhenheng's fourteenth-century medical synthesis, which in turn shaped later medical doctrines. Liu's discussions also contributed to making dian and kuang two quasi identical illnesses.

Liu Wansu was born in northern China under Song Huizong (r. 1100-1126), the famous painter-emperor whose sumptuous reign ended when he lost half of his empire to northern invaders, the Jurchens who founded the Jin dynasty in 1115. [1] From his mid-twenties, Liu pored through Wang Bing's annotated version of the Basic Questions and became engrossed in the complexity of its immensely influential cosmological chapters. [2] To those tenacious enough to decipher them, these chapters explained the convoluted workings of the “five circulatory phases and six seasonal influences” (wuyun liuqi 五運六氣; often referred to as yunqi) as they applied to medicine. [3] The “five circulatory phases” were Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, and Water, the Five Agents familiar to those who have studied any aspect of Chinese thought. The six types of climatic Qi were Wind 風, Heat 熱, Dampness 濕, Fire 火 (or Summer Heat 署), Dryness 燥, and Cold 寒.

Wuyun liuqi provided tools to detect regularities within unfolding processes and to intervene effectively in these processes. Liu Wansu used the fluid interactions between the Five Agents as a guide for scripting both physiological and pathological processes. [8] The Five Agents and the five Yin viscera (五臟) interacted in a way illustrated synoptically in Figure 4.1 (next page). This system was homeostatic (it had an inherent tendency to equilibrium) but dynamic. Since all of its elements were inter-related, a slight imbalance (be it excess or deficiency) in any of the Five Agents or organs led to illnesses that could affect the entire organism. By a sequence of effects predicted by the model, an excess of emotions could, for instance, lead to hemiplegia:

Hemiplegia caused by Wind strokes [occurs] because Cardiac Fire abruptly becomes excessive, and [Kidney] Water decays and is unable to curb it. Fire can thus overcome Metal, as a result of which Metal can no longer overcome Wood: Liver Wood thus becomes excessive of its own and joins with the heat of the Fire, causing [the] sudden and violent collapse [that is characteristic of Wind strokes]. Sudden illnesses often result from excesses in the Five Wills and Seven Emotions.[^1]

sample_paragraphs: ## “Danxi said…” The textual life of medical ideas, 1360-1530
“Danxi said…” The textual life of medical ideas on madness, 1360-1530

Danxi said that dian belongs to Yin and kuang to Yang, that dian is excessive joy and kuang excessive anger. He also stated that the doubling of Yin is dian and the doubling of Yang is kuang. 丹溪謂癲屬陰 狂屬陽 癲多喜 狂多怒 又云重陰者癲 重陽者狂
Xu Chunfu 徐春甫 in Gujin yitong daquan 古今醫統大全 (1556) [1]

Chapters 3 and 4 traced a momentous transformation in the etiology of madness from Wind to internal Fire and mucus between the twelfth and the fourteenth century. The Ming dynasty (1368-1644) was not a period of strong epistemological breaks in medicine, but one in which physicians re-orchestrated earlier approaches to form new doctrinal and therapeutic emphases. Xu Chunfu above was citing the Danxi xinfa 丹溪心法, a composite work compiled and printed in his own Huizhou Prefecture (Anhui) in the early 1480s and that quickly became the most influential work attributed to Zhu Zhenheng 朱震亨 ("Danxi" 丹溪: 1282-1358). This and the next chapter show how the development of Ming medical thinking on dian and kuang was shaped by three important trends that are well symbolized by Xu's quotation: the rising influence of precepts attributed to Danxi, the importance of Huizhou as a center of medical theorizing and publication, and the profound intertextuality of the elite medical tradition.
5.1 Intertextual composition and the Danxi corpus
The “Danxi corpus” in the history of medical thinking on madness

The rise to prominence of a body of teachings attributed to Zhu Zhenheng deeply shaped Ming medical thinking and practice. Zhu's teachings appeared in a wide array of texts books and manuscripts by Zhu, notes by his disciples, works attributed to Zhu that were collated after his death by people who had known him, and later anthologies based on a mix of the previous elements and a dose of interpretation of what Zhu might have thought. These works were compiled and printed from the second half of the fourteenth century to about 1600, when the last book attributed to Zhu was published. I refer to these texts as the "Danxi corpus" because most of them contained Zhu's literary name "Danxi" in their title. If there was ever a Danxi school of medicine, it should refer to this body of works and to the physicians whose training, doctrinal thinking, and clinical practice were guided by them.

The Danxi corpus was one major channel through which the reinterpretation of madness that I traced in the previous chapter was further systematized and became available to a large number of physicians. I will explain how, between 1360 and 1530, the Danxi corpus kept attributing madness to mucus and Fire and recommending treating pscho-behavioral pathology with purgatives or emetics.

For a number of interrelated reasons, these doctrines became the enduring basis from which physicians explained and treated madness for the rest of imperial history. The notion of “Wind” upon which the older etiologies had relied had been discredited. Few of the works that had attributed madness to Wind were reprinted, and a dominant hermeneutic strategy (discussed below) allowed doctors to ignore earlier works that were not consistent with current understandings. Finally, a few dispersed statements on madness came to be considered authoritative simply because they appeared in texts attributed to Danxi. These passages were bundled together in increasingly sophisticated sections on madness in the Danxi corpus, as well as in the works of the physicians who admired Danxi's works.
passages were bundled together in increasingly sophisticated sections on madness in the Danxi corpus, as well as in the works of the physicians who admired Danxi's works.

For my argument to be convincing, I must therefore demonstrate the ascendancy of Danxi precepts. Discursive dominance requires a certain density of social diffusion. Through texts and people (notably Zhu's own disciples), Zhu Zhenheng's medicine first spread like a rhizome along arteries such as the Grand Canal, feeding on social connections and networks of teachers and readers, growing more densely in some places than others, and presenting different faces in the many areas where it flourished. The Danxi corpus became dominant insofar as many important debates between medical specialists concerned the way in which Danxi's legacy should be interpreted. Physicians appropriated the name "Danxi" as a symbol of authority or used it as a foil to make their own doctrinal emphases appear more distinctive.

The diffusion of medical ideas took place in ways more complex than we can ever document. Knowledge and skills were transmitted through local teaching networks, some hereditary, others informal, and yet others based on strict ritual relations between a master and his (rarely her) disciples. [2] The vast majority of teachers remain undocumented. We know almost nothing about the routes by which medical books circulated throughout the empire, carried by traders, officials en route to their posts, or wandering physicians. The role of manuscripts and hand copies of printed books can only be surmised from notes made en passant in various writings, and the private letters that contributed to spreading new medical conceptions have almost all disappeared. [3] Finally we know too little about the oral teachings that made texts meaningful in particular teaching traditions, and about the process by which practitioners developed their skills through a mix of readings, instruction by one or several masters or seniors, and interaction with real patients. All these caveats make our understanding of received texts all the more important.

All these caveats make our understanding of received texts all the more important.
Intertextuality, zhezhong hermeneutics, and deliberate syncretism

To understand how the Danxi corpus was formed, we need to identify the textual provenance of the statements found therein. Different levels of inter-textuality can be distinguished. “Interdiscursivity” is the unwitting yet inevitable “intertext” that literary critiques identify even in the works of the most original authors. [4] Some consider it to be constitutive of any discourse, spoken or written. “Manifest intertextuality” occurs when writers explicitly attribute a passage to another source. The Ming medical tradition was intertextual in both of these senses, but here I pay particular attention to a third and somewhat different kind of intertextuality, not only in the way texts deployed common cultural motifs or overtly referred to previous works, but in the very way texts were produced—intertextuality as a method for assembling texts. [5]

Trying to prove the intertextuality of the Chinese medical literature may seem like laboring the obvious. After all, all texts everywhere are interdiscursively composed, and the authors I study never hid their reliance on previous works. Most literate Chinese traditions readily represented themselves as textually-based lineages of “transmission” (chuan 傳) and relied on one of the most intertextual devices imaginable—the commentary. But I believe too few have drawn the consequences of these practices seriously.
relied on one of the most intertextual devices imaginable—the commentary. But I believe too few have drawn the consequences of these practices seriously.

My intertextual approach draws attention to a notion whose importance has escaped most scholars: zbezhong (折衷 or 折中), which I shall leave untranslated for now. Paul Unschuld's widely consulted survey of Chinese medical ideas (1985: 203) contains a brief account of "an eclectic tradition known as the School of Compromise (zbezhong pai)," whose "followers did not propose any of their own theories, selecting instead those insights and instructions from the extensive medical literature that they found useful." Unschuld gave Li Zhongzi's 李中梓 (1588-1655) discussion of the Gate of Life (命門) as an example of eclectic thought and called Ni Weide 倪維德 (1303-1377) "one of the earliest eclectics." By claiming that the adherents of this purported school shared "the concern of numerous Confucians that medical knowledge could become so highly specialized that only experts would be able to master the field," he implied that these eclectics sought to assemble a smattering of knowledge for practical purposes with little effort to integrate the results.

I will show in this chapter that zbezbong was not a lesser school of casual gleaners (and actually not a school at all), but arguably the dominant hermenetic strategy and mode of textual composition of the most sophisticated medical writers of the age. Systematic treatises were the most intertextual of all, and syncretism was a sign of distinction rather than amateurism. Partly because of the doctrinally ambitious nature of medical writing from the twelfth century onwards, many contradictory claims on illness and vitality circulated, all rooted in compelling interpretations of the early medical canons. Only sophisticated thinkers (not “Confucian” non-specialists) could re-orchestrate such an intricate textual heritage into books. Zhu Zhenheng taught this syncretic approach to his students, and his disciples deployed it in their own writings. I will also show that $ \underline{\text{zhezhong}} $ hermeneutics and textual composition rested on the notion that illness was constantly changing.

sample_paragraphs: ## Replenish or attack? Competing etiologies and therapies of madness, 1530-1650
6 Replenish or attack? Competing etiologies and therapies of madness in Ming medicine
When there is depletion, replenish it; when there is repletion: drain it. 虛者補之 實者瀉之 Canon of Problems 難經, problem 69

This chapter explains the rich developments that took place in elite medical thinking and practice from roughly 1530 to 1650. In addition to writing long sections on diankuang in their treatises, physicians from this ebullient period recorded in some detail how they handled specific cases of madness. All of these men had read the Danxi xinfa 丹溪心法 (1482), knew of Wang Lun's 王綸 (1453-1510) arguments on Yin-replenishing, and embraced a syncretistic approach to past medical teachings. Their clinical practice and most of the doctrinal debates in which they engaged were thus informed by the trends in medical thinking that I described in previous chapters.

In the domain that interests us, the main event of the sixteenth century was perhaps the re-definition of dian 癲 as a form of madness characterized by non-manic symptoms and best treated by replenishing. The illness dian had existed since at least the third century BCE, and it had been associated with kuang since the first century BCE, but its main symptoms had first been close to those of epilepsy. When dian had been re-interpreted as a form of madness in the twelfth century, it had become so close to kuang in both etiology and symptoms that it could hardly be differentiated from kuang (3.4, 4.1). Dissatisfied with this confusion, many sixteenth-century physicians tried to reassert differences between dian and kuang. The clarifications proposed by a physician from Huizhou called Sun Yikui 孫一奎 (1522-1619) were eventually accepted by most elite physicians in the following centuries.

symptoms that it could hardly be differentiated from kuang (3.4, 4.1). Dissatisfied with this confusion, many sixteenth-century physicians tried to reassert differences between dian and kuang. The clarifications proposed by a physician from Huizhou called Sun Yikui 孫一奎 (1522-1619) were eventually accepted by most elite physicians in the following centuries.

One major area of discord between sixteenth-century physicians was whether mad behavior should be treated with purges and induced vomiting (which had been the prototypical treatments since at least the fourteenth century) or by replenishing. Attacking cures usually weakened the patient, whereas replenishing aimed to protect vital forces. I use “replenish or attack” to refer succinctly to debates concerning the relative merits of these two strategies and to clinical competition between them, both in general and in insanity cases. I will show that these debates on therapy usually depended on reflections concerning the nature and sources of human vitality as well as the proper ways to treat “depletion Fire,” a kind of pathological Fire triggered by an underlying organic depletion.

As I will argue, the newly reshaped dian—a type of madness caused by depletion—developed in a rich eco-system that included debates on vitality, controversies on the proper way to treat depletion Fire, reflections on the pathology of emotions, and the perceived need to resolve contradictions between current usage—dian and kuang as similar illnesses—and textual sources that presented dian and kuang as complementary opposites.

The “medical case files” (yian 醫案) on which I rely to study the dynamics of therapeutic practice were more than illustrations of medical doctrine. These records of clinical encounters described specific symptoms instead of the prototypical ones found in general treatises. They also provide information on the social and moral significance of madness and on gender differences in the treatment of an illness that treatises typically portrayed as un-gendered and morally neutral. By revealing the methods physicians used to treat mad people, case collections also tell us what parts of treatise descriptions that doctors found useful. The interactions between doctrinal knowledge and clinical practice—and the related but not entirely similar relations between treatises and collections of case files—are also themes that structure this chapter.

The interactions between doctrinal knowledge and clinical practice—and the related but not entirely similar relations between treatises and collections of case files—are also themes that structure this chapter.

I start by explaining the flourishing of medical case files in the sixteenth century, as well as their significance for the study of Chinese medical history. Starting in the 1520s, a few doctors used case data to question the conception of vitality that underlay the attacking therapies that had dominated early-Ming treatments of madness. My second section focuses on Wang Ji 汪機 (1463-1540), an early critic who recorded his distinctive treatment of two insane people. The following two sections explore how two themes from Wang's writings were exploited later in the sixteenth century. Part 3 explains how a therapeutic strategy called "calorific replenishing" (wenhu 溫補) emerged from debates about the sources of human vitality and the proper way to treat "depletion Fire." I then analyze the increased attention that many physicians from Huizhou in Anhui (including Wang Ji) paid to emotional disorders and the therapeutic use of emotions.

All the above developments—the proliferation of case files, the association of madness with emotions, the rise of new views of vitality and the concurrent emergence of calorific replenishing, and the continuing practice of composing medical treatises by culling passages from existing sources—converged to create the new madness prototype dian. But this concept did not stabilize immediately. Section 5 explains how some physicians (many of whom were from Huizhou) attempted to distinguish dian from kuang on new grounds now that doctors commonly took both to refer to mad behavior. The sixth section shows that Sun Yikui's 孫一奎 (1522-1619) deliberations on the differences between dian, kuang, and xian built on the reflections of fellow Huizhou physicians and borrowed from other texts. His distinctions between dian and kuang were widely adopted later, notably by Wang Kentang 王肯堂 (1552-1638), whose enhancement of Sun's ideas I explain in section 7.

The rest of the chapter explains why the new notion of dian as a kind of madness caused by depletion did not become dominant. Zhang Jiebin 張介賓 (1563-1640), for example, defended calorific replenishing and scorchingly criticized previous conceptions of Fire, but still argued that madness was chiefly caused by Fire and should be treated with attacking drugs. In this chapter's last segment, I show that Li Zhongzi's 李中梓 (1588-1655) use of both attacking and replenishing drugs to treat kuang integrated the most common treatment for madness with concerns for preserving vitality.

This chapter shows how themes that had first developed in general reflections on pathology and vitality found their way into medical approaches to madness, first in individual cases, and eventually into treatises, where these new approaches were solidified. Scheme transfer thus remained the most important mode of change in the medical understanding and treatment of madness in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
6.1 The art of diagnosis and the rise of “medical case files” (yi’an 醫案)

Hans Ågren once remarked that Chinese physicians “did not use names of disorders as targets of therapy as in the West” (1982: 574). As Nathan Sivin (1987: 175) expounded, “The point of diagnosis in the early classics is not so much naming the illness as determining its manifestations.... and the dynamic character of pathological changes under way.” Many indeed consider that Chinese medicine does not recognize essential illnesses, but “a multiplicity of symptomatic transformations” (Furth 1992: 769). Let me briefly historicize this attention to “the dynamic character of pathological changes” and explain how it relates to the emergence of case files as a kind of medical publication.

The notion that illnesses were constantly changing started to emerge in the late eleventh century when a few physicians applied to other disorders models that had been designed to understand Cold Injury. A prototypical case of Cold Injury unfolded in distinct stages that each called for a different treatment. Xu Shuwei's 許叔微 (1079-1154) Ninety Discussions on Cold Injury (Shanghan jiushi lun 傷寒九十論), written at the turn in the twelfth century but only printed for the first time in the nineteenth century, were early accounts of successful treatments based on unique diagnoses.[^1]

Zhang Yuansu 張元素 (12 $ ^{th} $ cent.) and his disciples were among the first to stress in their teachings that doctors should design prescriptions only after having determined what imbalance was causing the symptoms at hand (4.3). Zhu Zhenheng 朱震亨 (1282-1358) presented this clinical flexibility as central to his own medicine, while emphasizing that he had learned this style of prescription from his master Luo Zhiti 羅知悌 (1238?-1327; 4.4). The variability of illness was also made plausible by the doctrine of the “Five periods and Six Qi” (highly influential in medical circles starting in the late eleventh century), which postulated that cosmic phenomena, disease, and human vital forces varied according to natural cycles. This cosmological scheme was enthusiastically supported by Liu Wansu 劉完素 (ca. 1120 – ca. 1200; 4.1), Zhang Yuansu, and Zhang Congzheng 張從正 (1156-1228; 4.2) and remained prominent in medical thinking well into the Ming dynasty (1368-1644).

Most elite physicians from the twelfth century onward, while recognizing that there was “constancy” (chang 常) to illnesses, emphasized that the best healers should also react to “transformations” (bian 變), the events that diverged from the regular ways in which reality was supposed to unfold. “Constancy” itself referred not to unchanging essences but to the regular and predictable way in which processes developed.

sample_paragraphs: ## Shapes of practices Medical trends surrounding dian and kuang, 1650-1911
Shapes of practice
Medical trends surrounding dian and kuang, 17th-19th century

The profusion of medical works that appeared after 1650 are an irritating windfall. As medical publications boomed, vectors of knowledge transmission and the doctrinal debates that interested physicians became more intricate and numerous. It thus becomes difficult to find narrative threads to explain how Qing medical reflections on madness changed. Far too many texts were published for me to base my conclusions on comprehensive data as I tried to do for earlier periods. But the extensive array of short treatises, collections of case files, formularies, and medical primers that appeared in Qing times hint to the thinking and practice of minor physicians who made no “contributions to the development of Chinese medicine”—to borrow a phrase from a less critical historiography. These works allow us to see how much medical luminaries had in common with their less famous counterparts.

I first present a few important trends in Chinese medical thinking and practice from the seventeenth to the nineteenth century. After showing that the mucus etiology remained dominant over that period, I show how resilient and ubiquitous the script of blockage of the Heart by mucus was. I map the vivid “imagination of mucus” [1] through which physicians—from treatise writers to village healers—continued to envision madness from the seventeenth to the nineteenth century. I then turn to a pivotal figure in eighteenth-century medicine—Ye Gui 葉桂 (1667-1746)—and to what an influential work attributed to him said about madness. Next, I explain how nineteenth-century physicians (a number of whom proclaimed their admiration for Ye Gui) turned the Liver into a new pathological nexus and eventually claimed that madness and emotional disorders were rooted in Liver imbalances. Then I outline how Qing medical writers increasingly distinguished dian from kuang by symptoms instead of etiology, and how this displacement eventually provoked another transformation in the meaning of dian. The last section concerns a physician called Wu Tang 吳瑭 (1758-1836), another admirer of Ye's approaches, who claimed to have cured several mad patients. I translate and analyze one of his cases at some length, focusing on the dynamics of therapy and the efficacy of the drug-based treatments he deployed.

This chapter is the last of six chronological chapters about medical approaches to madness. It shows what approaches Chinese physicians adopted on the eve of the state's intervention in redefining "Chinese medicine" in the twentieth century, and explains what conceptions and treatments were contemporaneous with the laws on "killing because of madness" whose emergence I explain in Chapter 11. 7.1 Qing medical trends
Danxi and the other "masters"

By the early seventeenth century, “Danxi”—the label by which doctors referred to precepts and methods they attributed to Zhu Zhenheng 朱震亨 (1282-1358; 4.4)—was no longer the awe-inspiring name it had been a hundred years earlier, and the “Danxi corpus” no longer shaped medical debates. [2] Physicians gave less credence to Danxi’s views of vitality.

which they summarized as “Yang is in excess, Yin in deficit” (陽有餘陰不足). Zhu’s reflections on vitality had been criticized by advocates of “calorific replenishing” (6.3), but even those who opposed warm-replenishing therapies did not return to Zhu’s conceptions.

Danxi precepts had become popular partly thanks to the easy availability of user-friendly treatises like the Danxi xinfa 丹溪心法 (1482; see 5.5). In the seventeenth century, however, new primers like Gong Tingxian's 龔廷賢 compilations (late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries) and the works of Li Zhongzi 李中梓 (1588-1655) started to displace Danxi works. They remained popular into the nineteenth century (see 7.4).

Just as the works of Danxi and other masters from the twelfth to fourteenth centuries stopped being reprinted, Zhang Ji's 張機 Treatise on Cold Injury and Essentials of the Golden Casket (third century) became the main focus of medical studies. One trace of the shift in prominence from Danxi toward Zhang Ji was the severance of Zhang from a group of specialists with which Ming physicians had associated him. Wang Lun 王綸 (1463-1510) had coined the phrase “the four masters” (四子) to refer to Zhang Ji 張機 (d. ca. AD 220), Liu Wansu 劉完素 (ca. 1120-1200), Li Gao 李昇 (1181-1256), and Zhu Zhenheng, who Wang claimed had each perfected therapies for one kind of disorder. [3] Li Zhongzi (1588- 1655) later called the same men the “four great experts” (四大家). [4] It was probably Suzhou doctor Zhang Lu 張璐 (1617-1699) who first wrote of “the four great experts of the Jin and Yuan” (金元四大家), a group in which he included Zhang Congzheng 張從正 (1156-1228) instead of Zhang Ji, observing that Zhang Ji should not be placed among doctors he had influenced. Zhang Lu saw the doctrines of these “four masters” as considerably inferior to Zhang Ji’s. Many surveys of Chinese medical history note that Qing doctors studied the Treatise on Cold Injury intensely, [5] but they are usually silent about the shift away from Jin-Yuan medicine that this new concentration on Zhang Ji implied.

[4] It was probably Suzhou doctor Zhang Lu 張璐 (1617-1699) who first wrote of “the four great experts of the Jin and Yuan” (金元四大家), a group in which he included Zhang Congzheng 張從正 (1156-1228) instead of Zhang Ji, observing that Zhang Ji should not be placed among doctors he had influenced. Zhang Lu saw the doctrines of these “four masters” as considerably inferior to Zhang Ji’s. Many surveys of Chinese medical history note that Qing doctors studied the Treatise on Cold Injury intensely,[^1] but they are usually silent about the shift away from Jin-Yuan medicine that this new concentration on Zhang Ji implied.

For Zhang Ji this new autonomy was an astonishing promotion, since his works were now discussed on a par with the Inner Canon, which for centuries had been treated as the ultimate source of medical knowledge. [6] In a 1732 preface to one of You Yi's 尤怡 (d. 1749) many works on Zhang Ji's medicine, Xu Dachun 徐大椿 (1693-1771) ridiculed the common concept that Zhang had specialized only in the treatment of Cold Injury and that he could be put on the same (low) footing as Liu Wansu, Li Gao, and Zhu Zhenheng. [7] Xu developed this idea a few years later in a pugnacious assessment of the “four great experts” in his Treatise on the Origin and Currents of Medical Studies (Yixue yuanliu lun 醫學源流論; 1757). [8] Chen Xiuyuan 陳修園 (1753-1823) also adopted Zhang Lu's new interpretation of the “four masters” in his Three-Character Classic of Medicine (Yixue san zì jìng 醫學三字經; 1804), pointing out that Li Zhongzi's interpretation of them as including Zhang Ji was “erroneous” (誤). [9]

Qing Suzhou was an important center of medical studies supported by a prosperous printing industry and mature scholarly networks. As one of the main cities on the Grand Canal, it had long been an important hub of trade and communication, and many doctors had traveled there to find books and exchange ideas. But in Qing times Suzhou physicians claimed to represent the most advanced medical approaches in the empire. Although this pride predated the eighteenth century, it became particularly evident after the publication in 1766 of some of Ye Gui's 葉桂 (1667-1746; see 7.5 below) case files by men who claimed to be his disciples. I discuss Suzhou doctors' approach to madness in the next chapter. [10]

One trend in the eighteenth and especially the nineteenth century was the rising number of case collections in the surviving medical literature. Many of them were never printed. They allow us to continue comparing the propositions found in treatises with the way physicians actually handled mad patients. Through them, we can also understand better how women were treated when they behaved in ways that were identified as mad (see Ch. 9).
Many practices I described in previous chapters persisted into the Qing period.

Competition between physicians and rivalry between therapies continued unabated and may even have sharpened as doctors grew in numbers. As some kept replenishing their patients with warming drugs, others kept blaming them for it, as when Xu Yuhe 許豫和 (late 18 $ ^{th} $ century) accused a physician of having exacerbated a madman’s symptoms with calorific replenishing, or when Wu Tang 吴塘 (1758-1836) claimed that another doctor’s attacking of mucus and Fire in a case of insanity had “helped the bandits do harm” (助賊為虐). [11]

Medical writing also remained profoundly intertextual. Several treatises from the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries included long and increasingly complex sections on madness. They were longer and denser partly because they could borrow from a larger number of texts, but also because they applied to more disorders than ever the old claim that any illness could be caused by multiple factors. Two representative examples are Feng Zhaozhang's 馮兆張 (from Haiyan 海鹽 in Zhejiang) Jinnang milu zazheng daxiao becan 錦囊祕錄雜證大小合參 (in 20 juan; 1694) and Shen Jin'ao's 沈金鰲 (1717-1776; from Wuxi 無錫 in Jiangsu) Zabing yuanliu xizhu 雜病源流犀燭 (in 30 juan; 1773), both of which concentrated on explaining miscellaneous illnesses.

Besides these exhaustive accounts of manifold etiologies, we find attempts to simplify—even unify—medical doctrines, books with titles like Unity in the Forest of Medicine (Luo Denggao's 駱登高 Yilin yizhi 醫林一致; 1703), Knowing Medicine in One Glance (Zhu Shijin's 朱時進 Yijian nengyi 一見能醫; 1769), and Medicine for Sots (Long Huitang's 龍繪堂 Chunzi yi 蠢子醫; 1882). Their authors tried to distinguish these handbooks from difficult treatises such as those I mentioned in the previous paragraph. Let us now turn more directly to madness, starting with the way Qing physicians defined kuang in relation to dian.

sample_paragraphs: ## Ghosts or mucus? Possession symptoms and their treatment in Ming and Qing medicine
Ghosts or mucus?
Possession symptoms and their treatments in Ming and Qing medicine
I also saw a bearded figure lifting my oilcloth screen, but he suddenly disappeared. I was startled and I started to feel befuddled inside: I wanted to seek death. 又見一鬍子將油簾揭起 倏忽不見 吃了一驚 心內恍 惚起來 自欲尋死
Licentiate Xu Ding 徐鼎, recounting a vision (1768) [1]
How can demonic affliction make people sick! It is just that some disorders look like demonic affliction. 鬼祟豈能病人 不過病似鬼祟耳
Yu Zhen 俞震 in a note to a medical case file (1778) [2] 8.1 Spectral affliction in late-imperial medicine

Qing men and women often caught sight of “ghosts” and felt the result of their malicious actions. To banish these demons, the relatives of afflicted people could hire rituals specialist, doctors who claimed they could oust specters with drugs, or physicians like Yu Zhen who denied the demonic etiology altogether, but claimed they knew methods to cure possession symptoms. Chapter 13 will explain in more detail the ways in which common people tried to cure their mad-acting relatives, including cases in which they sought the help of both exorcists and physicians.

In this chapter, I discuss the ways in which physicians explained and handled symptoms that resembled those of involuntary possession. [3] By possession, I refer to invasion by a non-human (or no longer human) force that could supposedly control the thoughts, acts, and speech of their victim. Possession was expressed by verbs like ping 憑, yi 依, or fu 附, which meant “attaching to” or “relying upon” a person. Ghosts were also often said to “enter” (ru 入) the body of their victims. All these terms were not part of specialized medical terminology, but physicians used them when they discussed cases of “possession.”

Regardless of whether they believed in ghosts, most scholarly healers included sections on “demonic affliction” (鬼祟), “affliction by evil” (邪祟), “spectral illnesses” (祟病), or “evil demons” (邪鬼) in their treatises or case collections. Ancient texts had attributed all kinds of ailments to spirits, from toothaches to painful childbirth. [4] Most late-imperial doctors, however, attributed to ghostly possession chiefly a cluster of symptoms that looked like those of madness. These “possession symptoms” included delirium, strange speech, unprovoked grief, extreme apathy, hallucinations and the desire to injure oneself.

The concept of sui 崇 is almost as old as the Chinese writing system itself. Donald Harper has glossed sui (in ancient usage) as a calamity brought about by spirits in response to human conduct of which they disapproved. [5] Because of the several layers of meaning it acquired through time, sui is difficult to translate, but for late imperial times I shall gloss it as “specter” or “spectral affliction,” or as “affliction” when it occurs in compounds like xiesui 邪祟 (“affliction by evil”) and guisui 鬼祟 (“demonic affliction”).

We know from oracle-bone inscriptions that the ruling elite of the Shang “dynasty” (16 $ ^{th} $-11 $ ^{th} $ century BCE) had attributed most illnesses to curses (sui) by royal ancestors (Unschuld 1985: 19-28). By late imperial times, the possible sources of such misfortunes had diversified: they could now be caused by the souls of dead people, by shape-shifting animal spirits (often foxes), and by the looming population of goblins and malicious wraiths that were thought to roam along thoroughfares or near old temples. The ghosts of the dead typically looked menacingly hirsute, but “foxes” preferred to assume well-trimmed human shapes—alluring emanations that could dupe maidens and make scholars drool.

Whereas ritual texts that proposed methods to remove these beings gave little detail about how they affected the body, medical sources often described ghosts as entering the body of their victims and occupying specific organs. As such, late-imperial sui (“spectral afflictions”) thus differed from the sui (“calamities”) of the Shang era, which did not depend on control over the body of the victim. [6]

This chapter broadens the sphere of “madness” as an object of historical inquiry. Although “mad” behavior could be understood in different ways, people who construed such behavior differently still knew that they were discussing the same acts. I aim to show that no two approaches to these symptoms were inherently incompatible, and that all of them could be blended through practice, as when physicians claimed they could treat possession with drugs, or when they argued that ghosts triggered a series of pathological reactions identical to those that occurred during purely organic illnesses.

To emphasize the uncertainty that existed in many people's minds about whether crazy acts were caused by illness or demonic invasion, I first explain how the symptoms of possession resembled the manifestations of medically understood insanity. I then discuss Zhu Zhenheng's 朱震亨 (1282-1358) influential view that possession symptoms were commonly triggered by mucus. [7] The third section tries to interpret the dramatic decrease in mentions of exorcistic healers in late-imperial cases that physicians or their patients' relatives explicitly attributed to "evil ghosts" or designated as "spectral affliction." I suggest that shamans and elite physicians no longer competed for the same patients. Yet, as I show in the fourth section, even in the late nineteenth century many elite physicians still ascribed illness to the action of various kinds of ghosts. The "medical exorcisms" they performed often borrowed from ritual therapies that today we associate more readily with Daoism than with scholarly medicine. [8] The final section explains how some physicians explained and treated hallucinations, a special type of possession symptom.
8.2 The ambiguous closeness of madness and possession symptoms

People from the times and places I study often found resemblances between what they called dian or kuang and what they called “spectral affliction” (sui). These categories were not equivalent, but both specialists and commoners found them meaningfully related in a number of contexts. First, acts designated as “mad” could be attributed to possession, because the terms that meant “madness” did not necessarily entail a medical explanation. Even “illnesses” (bing病) were not always explained in ways we would call medical. Taoist texts routinely attributed “madness” (diankuang 颠狂) to possession and proposed treatments for it. Diankuang was one of the many ills that texts from the Daofa buiyuan 道法會元—a ritual compendium probably compiled in the early 15 $ ^{th} $ century—professed they could treat. [9] Some passages warned that many kinds of spirits could make people crazy. [10] Yongcui 李用粹 wrote an entry called “Madness resembles spectral affliction” (癫狂似祟)

Others called “mad words and blithe speech” kinds of “spectral afflictions” (狂言妄语…
此等之祟) and said that “specters with a form… render people mad” (諸有形之祟…令人

sample_paragraphs: ## Gendered mania Women’s madness in late-imperial medicine
Gendered mania? Women's madness in late-imperial case records

A notorious adage circulating in late imperial medical circles declared that the women's illnesses were more difficult to cure than men's. [1] Two other sayings claimed that women's bodies were "governed by Blood" (以血為主 or a variant) and that treating women necessitated "separate prescriptions" (别方). Ming and Qing physicians cited these sayings to set up concurring arguments, to introduce objections or qualifications, or to clinch points with the help of a well-formulated piece of common knowledge.

In this chapter, I want to explore whether the gender of the sufferer was one of the fault lines along which the understanding and treatment of mad acts and mad people were divided. Did physicians from the Song (960-1279) to the Qing (1644-1911) describe madness as occurring to women by different mechanisms than to men? Did the treatments they prescribed differ according to the gender of the patient? What other aspects of medical approaches to insanity were “gendered”?

Since mad behavior was obviously less frequent than menses and pregnancy, relatively few cases of madness where the patient was a woman have survived. Many arguments in this chapter are based on 35 case files—from 23 physicians—of female patients who suffered from mad symptoms (see Table 9.1 next page), as well as a few general comments in medical treatises about how madness occurred to women. I selected cases from the twelfth to the early twentieth century that appeared in sections on madness of case collections, as well as other cases in which women were said to be suffering from kuang or dian or in which their behavior was described as kuang or dian, and finally cases that did not conform with the above criteria but in which the symptoms corresponded with those mentioned in descriptions of dian and kuang, that is, manic running, discarding of clothes, excessive anger or grief, and the like. Since it would be cumbersome to reinsert each case in its intellectual and social context, I will refer to relevant sections in other chapters for more information on the physicians who wrote these cases. I consider “postpartum madness” as distinct, and I therefore discuss it in its own section at the end of this chapter.

Since the cases span more than 800 years, the problem of change inevitably poses itself, albeit a bit intractably since my sample for each period is so meager. There is an average of 4 cases per century and barely more than 2 if we exclude the last hundred years I cover. I found only two relevant cases between 1588 and 1821. The 35 cases represent the way elite doctors (mostly from the Lower Yangzi region) explained the way they understood and treated mad women. They give only a small glimpse of how society handled women who were called mad. Indeed, the main treatment for manic women may not have been medical. There is too little evidence to tell, but home confinement was certainly an option, though it may have come only after the failure of medical or exorcistic treatments. Since the documents tell us precious little about the way female patients experienced their own condition, we are also deprived of the “first-person” data that have informed recent studies of women in Chinese history. [2] I will remind the reader of these limits when I propose tentative conclusions or try to point to possible trends.

The 35 cases represent the way elite doctors (mostly from the Lower Yangzi region) explained the way they understood and treated mad women. They give only a small glimpse of how society handled women who were called mad. Indeed, the main treatment for manic women may not have been medical. There is too little evidence to tell, but home confinement was certainly an option, though it may have come only after the failure of medical or exorcistic treatments. Since the documents tell us precious little about the way female patients experienced their own condition, we are also deprived of the “first-person” data that have informed recent studies of women in Chinese history. [2] I will remind the reader of these limits when I propose tentative conclusions or try to point to possible trends.

This chapter’s opening section tries to determine whether and how the diagnoses and therapies of “mad women” were gendered. One guiding issue will be whether physicians found relevant the notion that the body of women was “governed by Blood.” The second section focuses on nudity and excessive desires, two symptoms that were likely to provoke extra-medical responses. Perhaps unsurprisingly, we shall see that the gendered character of medical encounters could go beyond the issue of how the body itself was understood. Third and finally, I present medical interpretations of “postpartum madness,” a form of insanity that could (by definition) only happen to women. I explain how postpartum madness was theorized and handled, and how it was understood in relation to similar symptoms happening to men and non-parturient women. For my purpose, it makes no difference whether postpartum insanity was “really madness,” since late-imperial physicians tied it explicitly to what they called madness.

Medical explanations of mad behavior in treatises purported to apply to both men and women. But in practice, did doctors consistently trace cases of women's mad behavior to the roots they identified in their treatises? Did their descriptions and treatments apply to the "androgynous body" (Furth 1999: 25-29, 44-48 and 56-57)—a body without anatomical sex—that characterized elite Chinese medicine? Charlotte Furth has indeed argued that late-imperial physicians focused increasingly less on the uniqueness of women, and tended to understand the women's illnesses in the same way as they understood men's.

I shall agree with Furth in general, but I will also show that the etiology of madness was already ungendered in the Song dynasty (960-1279), and that glimpses of gendered etiologies only appeared in late-imperial times, especially in the nineteenth century. In recorded symptoms, identified etiology, and adopted therapy, a spectrum of more or less gendered solutions were available. Some symptoms (notably nudity and grief) were proportionally more common in women's cases, probably because these acts were seen as socially more problematic, and were therefore more likely to be brought to the attention of a physician. But although many nineteenth-century cases of mad women did not conform to what treatises said about insanity, most of them did. [3]

In both etiology and treatment, extant cases of “mad women” predating 1500 are indistinguishable from those of men. Xu Shuwei 許叔微 (1079-1154) gave the same pill to a woman who had been scared out of her wits by pirates and to a man who had lost his mind as he was about to be executed as a criminal. Wang Haogu 王好古 (13 $ ^{th} $ century) cured a manic woman with a purgative he borrowed from the Treatise on Cold Injury. [4] Two cases by Ni Weide 倪維德 (1303-1377) displayed the same gender neutrality. [5] If these physicians made distinctions between genders, they did not record them in their case files.

Even one of the best-known Song works on women's illnesses proposed solutions that were equally applicable to men. Chen Ziming's 陳自明 All-Inclusive Excellent Recipes for Women (Furen daquan liangfang 婦人大全良方; hereafter Excellent Recipes), which he compiled in the mid thirteenth century, regrouped a large number of recipes designed to treat disorders as they happened to women. [6] On the issue that concerns us, Chen maintained that, "In women, the disorders dian and kuang are brought about by the deviant [Qi] of Wind, which is absorbed when Qi and Blood are depleted" (夫婦人顛狂病者 由血氣虛受風邪所為也). [7] Despite the mention of Blood depletion, this etiology was not gendered, because it corresponded with the traditional etiology of most Wind disorders. [8]

In a brief case record, Chen explained that he cured a woman with the “Elixir that nourishes the correct” (養正丹), a common remedy for madness and seizures. [9] But as if to emphasize that this treatment was not designed exclusively for women, Chen mentioned that he also cured a man with the same remedy. Despite the popularity of Chen’s Excellent Recipes after Xue Ji 薛己 (1487-1559) re-edited them in 1547, there is no sign that Chen’s explanation of women’s mad behavior was ever adopted by elite physicians of the sixteenth century and after, probably because the Wind explanation that Chen had embraced had by then been replaced by a script that traced most problems involving consciousness to the disorderly movements of Fire and mucus in and around the Heart. [10]

A few sixteenth-century cases tell us what therapies were current at the time. The physicians who designed them did not seem to think these remedies applied to women better than to men. Wu Qiu 吳球 (fl. 1520s-30s) traced a young woman's strange behavior (she "would cry or laugh, or run around naked, or shut the doors and speak a lot" (或哭或笑 或裸體而走 或閉戶而多言) to "harm caused by excessive ratiocination, [which made] the spirit unable to hold to its lodging" (思慮過傷 神不守舍也). [11] In the sixteenth century, this etiology typified medicine's increasing focus on "inner harm"—a category that included exhaustion, food scarcity or excesses, and emotional imbalances—and the devising of new ways to treat it. Wu's therapy based on human placenta differed from those proposed in contemporary books, but, as great specialist of medicinal drugs Li Shizhen 李時珍 (1518- 1593) maintained, placenta could “treat all cases of wasting disorders and extreme fatigue as well as loss of mind and bewilderment caused by dian and xian, in both men and women” (治男女一切虚損勞極 癲癇失志恍惚). [12] Wu also gave his patient the “Will-fixing pill” (定志丸) and a daily regimen of “Heart-replenishing decoction” (補心湯), a treatment that he recommended elsewhere in a general explanation of therapies for dian. [13] The way he handled his female patient was thus not significantly gendered. After 100 days of treatment, the young woman was married, and one year later she had a child. Although this outcome had been enabled by drugs that were designed to act on the body’s inner dynamics, the proof of the cure was social, and therefore gendered.

[12] Wu also gave his patient the “Will-fixing pill” (定志丸) and a daily regimen of “Heart-replenishing decoction” (補心湯), a treatment that he recommended elsewhere in a general explanation of therapies for dian. [13] The way he handled his female patient was thus not significantly gendered. After 100 days of treatment, the young woman was married, and one year later she had a child. Although this outcome had been enabled by drugs that were designed to act on the body’s inner dynamics, the proof of the cure was social, and therefore gendered.

Xue Ji's 薛己 (1487-1559) treatment of a young woman typified his "calorific-replenishing" (6.3) approach to many disorders. [14] His remark that other physicians had attempted to give her "Wind-mucus" drugs is another sign that gender-specific treatments may not have been common at the time, since, as we have seen, these drugs then represented the most conventional medical treatment for insanity. I can also find no meaningful gender distinctions between Wang Ji's 汪機 (1463-1540; see 6.2) two cases of madness caused by inner harm, one of a man and one of a woman. Wang's contrarian attribution of both cases to depletion of the Yang-brilliance tract shows that he was assuming that the bodies of men and women functioned in the same way.

Only in the late sixteenth century did a few physicians start to identify particular scenarios by which madness could happen to women. Li Chan's 李梴 Introduction to Medical Learning (Yixue rumen 醫學入門, 1575) explained that "when a woman's menstrual waters flow out in excess, Blood and Qi confuse the Heart; or when postpartum noxious dew flow out in excess, Blood and Qi confuse the Heart; or when postpartum noxious dew flushes upward and makes speech jumbled and the mind unable to stay steadfast, this is the result of depletion of Blood and exhaustion of Spirit” (有婦人月水崩漏過多 血氣迷心 或產後惡露上沖 而言語錯亂 神志不守者 此血虛神耗也). [15] Li's popular work was among the first to ascribe mad symptoms to pathological menses, but the text explained how one specific imbalance could lead to insanity, not how mad symptoms should be interpreted in general. In other words, he was locking one etiology and some symptoms together in a contextually limited script. Li probably believed that the general explanation of insanity as caused by the action of Fire and mucus still applied to women who did not suffer from menorrhagia and whose symptoms did not occur postpartum.
